draft.title: Rhetorical devices
card: repeating the same opening words in a run of sentences. A speaker might begin three sentences in a row with "We will".
grouping ideas in threes, such as "fast, fair and free". A list of three feels complete and is easy to remember.
setting opposite ideas side by side, such as "Small steps now, giant leaps later". The contrast makes the point stand out.
Speakers use these devices to make their words persuasive and memorable. Name the device, then explain its effect on the audience.
draft.remember: Repeat openings, group in threes, or set opposites together to be memorable.

a.q: A speaker says: "Learn today, lead tomorrow." Which device is mainly used?
opts: Antithesis, setting two opposite ideas side by side
Anaphora, repeating the opening words of sentences
Rule of three, grouping ideas into a set of three
Rhetorical question, asking an audience a question
a.why: Today and tomorrow are set against each other in one short line, which is antithesis. It is not anaphora, as no opening words are repeated.
a.clue: Look at the two time words in the line.

b.q: A captain tells her team: "We trained hard. We played smart. We never gave up." Which device does the repeated opening show?
opts: Anaphora, which builds rhythm and a sense of unity
Antithesis, which contrasts effort with the result
Antithesis, which sets the team against its rivals
Rule of three, which groups three adjectives together
b.why: Each sentence begins with the same word, "We", which is anaphora and builds rhythm and unity. The speech has three sentences, but the question asks about the repeated opening. Nothing in the speech is set as an opposite, so it is not antithesis.
b.clue: Look at how each sentence begins.

a.best: Antithesis, setting two opposite ideas side by side

b.best: Anaphora, which builds rhythm and a sense of unity
